front_blocks.md: Define **addition polymerisation**.

back_blocks.md: An **addition polymerisation** is a reaction in which many monomers containing at least one C=C double bond join together to form long polymer chains as the only product.

cards.back_md: An **addition polymerisation** is a reaction in which many monomers containing at least one C=C double bond join together to form long polymer chains as the only product.

front_blocks.md: What bond change occurs in the monomer during addition polymerisation?

back_blocks.md: The **π-bond** in the C=C double bond breaks. The monomers then link together to form new **C-C single bonds**, producing the polymer chain.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Addition polymerisation produces two products: the polymer and a small molecule such as water.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Addition polymerisation produces only one product — the polymer. No small molecules are released, which distinguishes it from condensation polymerisation.

front_blocks.md: In addition polymerisation, the small reactive molecules that join together are called **..........**. The long-chain molecule they form is called a **...........**.

back_blocks.md: In addition polymerisation, the small reactive molecules that join together are called **monomers**. The long-chain molecule they form is called a **polymer**.

front_blocks.md: Define **repeat unit**.

back_blocks.md: A **repeat unit** is the smallest group of atoms that, when connected one after another, makes up the polymer chain. It is shown in square brackets in structural and displayed formulae.

cards.back_md: A **repeat unit** is the smallest group of atoms that, when connected one after another, makes up the polymer chain. It is shown in square brackets in structural and displayed formulae.

front_blocks.md: How does the repeat unit of a poly(alkene) differ from its monomer?

back_blocks.md: The repeat unit is identical to the monomer except that the **C=C double bond** is replaced by a **C-C single bond**. The repeat unit shown in brackets in a displayed formula is not the monomer itself.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Poly(chloroethene), also known as PVC, is made by the addition polymerisation of chloroethene monomers.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
Chloroethene (CH<sub>2</sub>=CHCl) undergoes addition polymerisation. The C=C bond opens and the monomers link to form poly(chloroethene), commonly called PVC.

back_blocks.md: Locate the **repeat unit** shown inside square brackets. The monomer is the same as the repeat unit, but with the **C-C single bond** replaced by a **C=C double bond**.

front_blocks.md: Define **non-biodegradable**.

back_blocks.md: A **non-biodegradable** material is one that cannot be broken down by microorganisms. Poly(alkenes) are non-biodegradable and can take hundreds of years to decompose in landfill.

cards.back_md: A **non-biodegradable** material is one that cannot be broken down by microorganisms. Poly(alkenes) are non-biodegradable and can take hundreds of years to decompose in landfill.

front_blocks.md: Why are poly(alkenes) described as resistant to chemical attack?

back_blocks.md: Poly(alkenes) are very large **alkane-like molecules**. They are **unreactive** and do not undergo chemical reactions, making them **resistant to chemical attack** by most reagents.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Burning poly(alkenes) is an environmentally safe method of disposal because they combust completely to give only carbon dioxide and water.

back_blocks.md: **False.**

Burning poly(alkenes) produces harmful combustion products that pollute the environment. Complete combustion to CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O is not always achieved, and toxic gases can be released.

front_blocks.md: Give three reasons why the disposal of poly(alkenes) is a major environmental challenge.

back_blocks.md:
1. They are **unreactive** and resistant to chemical attack.
2. They are **non-biodegradable**, persisting in landfill for hundreds of years.
3. Burning them produces **harmful combustion products** that pollute the environment.

front_blocks.md: Define **landfill**.

back_blocks.md: **Landfill** is a method of waste disposal in which materials are buried underground. Non-biodegradable poly(alkenes) persist for hundreds of years in landfill, causing long-term environmental pollution.

front_blocks.md: What chemical property of poly(alkenes) makes them useful as plastics but also problematic for disposal?

back_blocks.md: Their **unreactivity** (resistance to chemical attack) makes them durable and useful as plastics. However, the same property means they are **non-biodegradable** and persist in the environment for very long periods.
